description: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language for creating the structure of web pages.

Introduction to HTML

One Shot Lecture Basic to Advance

What is HTML?

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard language used to create and structure web pages. HTML is not a programming language, but a markup language that uses tags to define content.

Why HTML is Important

  • Every website you visit is built using HTML.
  • It defines what appears on the page:
    • Text
    • Images
    • Videos
    • Links
    • Forms
  • HTML works together with:
    • CSS → Styling
    • JavaScript → Interactivity

How HTML Works

  1. HTML code is written in a .html file.
  2. A web browser reads this code.
  3. The browser renders the page visually for the user.

Self-Closing Tags

Some HTML tags do not need a closing tag because they do not have content inside.

  • <br> → Line break
  • <hr> → Horizontal rule
  • <img> → Image
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Sample Image">

Basic Structure of an HTML Document

Every HTML document follows a standard structure so that browsers can read and display it correctly. 

<!DOCTYPE html>
            <html lang="en">
            <head>
              <meta charset="UTF-8">
              <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
              <title>My First Web Page</title>
            </head>
            <body>
              <h1>Hello World!</h1>
              <p>This is my very first webpage.</p>
            </body>
            </html>

Summary

Concept Purpose
HTML Creates structure and content of web pages.
Tags Define specific elements (text, images, links, etc.).
Doctype Tells browser the version of HTML being used.
Head Metadata and configuration (not visible on page).
Body All visible content like text, images, and videos.

Basic HTML Tags

Tag Description Example
<!DOCTYPE html> Declares the document type and version of HTML. <!DOCTYPE html>
<html> Root element of the HTML document. <html> ... </html>
<head> Contains metadata and links to resources. <head> ... </head>
<title> Sets the title of the webpage. <title>My Page</title>
<meta> Provides metadata like charset or viewport settings. <meta charset="UTF-8">
<link> Links external resources like CSS files. <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<style> Defines internal CSS styles. <style> body { background: #fff; } </style>
<body> Contains all the visible page content. <body> ... </body>
<h1> - <h6> Headings, with <h1> being the largest and <h6> the smallest. <h1>Heading</h1>
<p> Defines a paragraph. <p>This is a paragraph.</p>
<br> Inserts a line break. Line 1<br>Line 2
<hr> Inserts a horizontal rule. <hr>
<a> Defines a hyperlink. <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
<img> Embeds an image. <img src="image.jpg" alt="Example">
<ul> & <li> Defines an unordered list and list items. <ul><li>Item</li></ul>
<ol> & <li> Defines an ordered list and list items. <ol><li>First</li></ol>
<div> A block-level container for grouping content. <div>Content</div>
<span> An inline container for styling text. <span>Highlighted text</span>
<strong> Represents strong importance (bold). <strong>Important</strong>
<em> Emphasizes text (italic). <em>Emphasized</em>
<table>, <tr>, <td>, <th> Creates a table, rows, and cells. <table> <tr><th>Name</th></tr> <tr><td>John</td></tr> </table>
<form> Creates a form for user input. <form action="#" method="post">...</form>
<input> Defines an input field. <input type="text">
<textarea> Multi-line text input field. <textarea>Text</textarea>
<button> Clickable button. <button>Click Me</button>
<label> Label for form elements. <label for="name">Name:</label>
<select> & <option> Dropdown menu with selectable options. <select><option>Option</option></select>
<script> Embeds or links JavaScript. <script>console.log('Hello');</script>
<header> Defines a header section. <header>Site Header</header>
<footer> Defines a footer section. <footer>Site Footer</footer>
<nav> Defines a navigation section. <nav><a href="#">Home</a></nav>
<section> Groups related content together. <section>Content Section</section>
<article> Independent self-contained content. <article>Article Content</article>
<aside> Side content related to main content. <aside>Related Info</aside>

1. HTML Document Structure

The basic structure of an HTML document includes <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body> tags.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p>Hello World!</p>
  </body>
</html>

Hello World!

HTML Attributes & Global Attributes

What is an Attribute?

An attribute gives extra information about an element. It always goes inside the opening tag and usually looks like name="value".

<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Visit Example</a>
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="A smiling student" width="300">
  • href tells a link where to go.
  • src tells an image or video where the file is.
  • alt is the text shown (or read aloud) when the image cannot be seen.
  • width / height set the size.

id vs class

These two attributes connect your HTML to CSS and JavaScript.

idclass
Unique?Yes, only one element per pageNo, many elements can share a class
Many values?NoYes, separate with spaces
CSS selector#main.card
Typical useLink target, one special element, JavaScript hookReusable styling
<h2 id="intro">Welcome</h2>
<p class="note highlight">This paragraph has two classes.</p>

Tip: choose names that describe what something is (price-tag), not how it looks (red-big-text).

Global Attributes

Global attributes work on every HTML element.

AttributePurposeExample
idUnique nameid="header"
classGroup for stylingclass="btn primary"
styleInline CSS (avoid for big styles)style="color:red"
titleTooltip on hovertitle="Click to save"
langLanguage of the contentlang="ur"
hiddenHides the elementhidden
tabindexKeyboard focus ordertabindex="0"
data-*Your own custom datadata-user-id="42"

Boolean Attributes

Some attributes are either on or off. If the name is present, it is on; you do not need a value.

<input type="text" required>
<input type="checkbox" checked>
<button disabled>Cannot click</button>

Live example:

data-* Attributes

Use data- attributes to attach small pieces of information to an element so JavaScript can read them later.

<button id="buy" data-product-id="101" data-price="499">Buy</button>

<script>
  const btn = document.getElementById("buy");
  console.log(btn.dataset.productId); // "101"
  console.log(btn.dataset.price);     // "499"
</script>

Notice that data-product-id becomes dataset.productId (camelCase) in JavaScript.

Best Practices

  • Write attribute names in lowercase.
  • Always put values in double quotes.
  • Keep ids unique.
  • Prefer classes in a CSS file over the style attribute.
  • Always add alt to images.

Semantic and Non-Semantic HTML Tags

Semantic tags in HTML clearly describe the meaning and purpose of the content they contain, making the code more readable, accessible, and SEO-friendly, such as <header>, <article>, <nav>, and <footer>. Non-semantic tags, like <div> and <span>, do not provide any inherent meaning and are mainly used for styling or grouping elements without indicating their role in the webpage structure.

Semantic and Non-Semantic Element

1. Semantic Tags

Semantic tags clearly describe their meaning in a human and machine-readable way. They improve SEO, accessibility, and code readability by providing context.

Examples of Semantic Tags

Tag Description
<header>Represents the header section of a webpage or a section.
<footer>Represents the footer section of a webpage or a section.
<article>Represents self-contained content like a blog post or news article.
<section>Represents a thematic grouping of content.
<nav>Represents a section for navigation links.
<aside>Represents secondary or sidebar content.
<main>Represents the main content of the document.
<figure>Represents self-contained content, such as images with captions.
<figcaption>Provides a caption for a <figure> element.
<mark>Highlights text for reference purposes.
<time>Represents a specific time or date.
<summary>A summary, often used with <details>.
<details>Used to create an expandable content area.

Example of Semantic HTML

<header>
  <h1>My Blog</h1>
  <nav>
    <a href="#home">Home</a>
    <a href="#about">About</a>
  </nav>
</header>

<main>
  <article>
    <h2>Semantic HTML Importance</h2>
    <p>Semantic tags make the web more accessible and structured.</p>
  </article>

  <aside>
    <h3>Related Articles</h3>
    <ul>
      <li><a href="#">HTML Basics</a></li>
      <li><a href="#">SEO Tips</a></li>
    </ul>
  </aside>
</main>

<footer>
  <p>© 2025 My Blog. All Rights Reserved.</p>
</footer>

2. Non-Semantic Tags

Non-semantic tags do not provide meaning about their content. They are used for styling or layout purposes only.

Examples of Non-Semantic Tags

Tag Description
<div>A generic block-level container used to group content.
<span>A generic inline container used to style specific text or content.

Example of Non-Semantic HTML

<div class="header">
  <div class="logo">My Blog</div>
  <div class="menu">
    <span>Home</span>
    <span>About</span>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="content">
  <div class="post">
    <span class="title">Semantic vs Non-Semantic Tags</span>
    <p>Using semantic tags makes your content more meaningful.</p>
  </div>
</div>

3. Comparison Between Semantic and Non-Semantic Tags

Aspect Semantic Tags Non-Semantic Tags
Definition Clearly describe the role and meaning of the content. Do not describe the meaning of the content.
SEO Benefit High — Helps search engines understand structure. Low — No added context for search engines.
Accessibility Improves accessibility for screen readers. No special accessibility benefits.
Readability Easier for developers to understand code structure. Harder to understand without CSS or comments.
Examples <header>, <footer>, <article>, <nav> <div>, <span>
Usage For structuring content meaningfully. For styling and layout purposes.

4. Using Both Together

Best practice is to use semantic tags for structure and non-semantic tags for styling or grouping when needed.

<header>
  <h1>My Website</h1>
  <nav>
    <a href="#home">Home</a>
    <a href="#contact">Contact</a>
  </nav>
</header>

<main>
  <section>
    <article>
      <h2>About Us</h2>
      <p>We build amazing websites using semantic HTML.</p>
    </article>
  </section>

  <aside>
    <div class="sidebar-box">
      <span>Advertisement</span>
    </div>
  </aside>
</main>

<footer>
  <p>© 2025 My Website</p>
</footer>

Div, Span, and Lists

The explanations of <div>, <span>, and HTML lists along with their example outputs.

1. The <div> Tag

<div> is a block-level element used to group larger sections of content.

<div class="container">
  <h2>Section Title</h2>
  <p>This is a block of content grouped inside a div.</p>
</div>

OUTPUT:

Section Title

This is a block of content grouped inside a div.

2. The <span> Tag

<span> is an inline element used to style small portions of text.

<p>This is a <span class="highlight">highlighted text</span> inside a paragraph.</p>

OUTPUT:

This is a highlighted text inside a paragraph.

3. HTML Lists

3.1 Ordered List (<ol>)

<ol>
  <li>First Item</li>
  <li>Second Item</li>
  <li>Third Item</li>
</ol>

  • Item C

<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>

2. HTML Form

In HTML, a form is a container that allows users to input data and submit it to a server for processing. Forms are essential for tasks like logging in, registering, searching, and submitting feedback. The <form> element wraps all the input fields and defines how the data will be sent.

HTML Input Types

  • text: Single-line text input.
  • password: Hidden characters for passwords.
  • email: Email format validation.
  • tel: Telephone number input.
  • url: Website URL input.
  • search: Search field input.
  • number: Numeric input only.
  • range: Slider for numeric values.
  • color: Color picker.
  • radio: Select one from multiple choices.
  • checkbox: Select one or more options.
  • file: Upload files.
  • date: Pick a date.
  • datetime-local: Select date and time.
  • month: Select month and year.
  • week: Select week and year.
  • time: Select time.
  • submit: Submit the form.
  • reset: Reset the form fields.
  • button: Generic button.
  • image: Image as a submit button.
  • hidden: Hidden input (invisible).

Example Form

<form>
  <label for="name">Name:</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name">

  <label for="email">Email:</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

  <label>Gender:</label>
  <input type="radio" name="gender" value="male"> Male
  <input type="radio" name="gender" value="female"> Female

  <label for="country">Country:</label>
  <select id="country" name="country">
    <option>USA</option>
    <option>UK</option>
    <option>India</option>
  </select>

  <label for="message">Message:</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message"></textarea>

  <input type="submit" value="Submit">
</form>

Output:

Male Female

Forms in Depth & Validation

Form Anatomy

A form collects data from the user. Each field needs a name (so the data has a label when it is sent) and a label (so the user knows what to type).

<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email">

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
  • action is where the data is sent.
  • method is get or post.
  • label for="email" connects to the input with id="email". Clicking the label focuses the input.

Choice Controls

<fieldset>
  <legend>Choose your course</legend>

  <label><input type="radio" name="course" value="html"> HTML</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="course" value="css"> CSS</label>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="newsletter"> Send me updates</label>

  <label for="level">Level</label>
  <select id="level" name="level">
    <option value="beginner">Beginner</option>
    <option value="advanced">Advanced</option>
  </select>

  <label for="bio">About you</label>
  <textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="3"></textarea>
</fieldset>
  • Radio buttons with the same name allow only one choice.
  • Checkbox allows many choices.
  • fieldset + legend group related fields for screen readers.

Useful Input Types

TypeWhat the browser gives you
emailChecks for an @ sign, mobile keyboard with @
numberOnly numbers, up/down arrows, min / max
telPhone keypad on mobile
urlChecks that the text looks like a URL
dateDate picker
rangeSlider
colorColour picker
fileFile chooser
passwordHides the characters

Built-in Validation

The browser can validate for you before the form is sent. Add these attributes:

AttributeMeaning
requiredField cannot be empty
minlength / maxlengthLimits for text length
min / maxLimits for numbers and dates
patternText must match a regular expression
type="email"Must look like an email address

Try it: leave fields empty or type something wrong, then press Submit.




<input id="code" name="code" type="text"
       pattern="[A-Za-z]{3}[0-9]{3}"
       title="Three letters followed by three digits" required>

GET vs POST

GETPOST
Data goes inThe URL (visible)The request body (hidden)
Good forSearching, filteringLogin, signup, uploads
Bookmarkable?YesNo
Safe for passwords?NeverYes (over HTTPS)

Important: Validate on the Server Too

Browser validation is only for convenience. Anyone can bypass it (for example by editing the page or sending the request directly). Your server must always check the data again. That is exactly why the Learning Hub API validates every signup and login request.

Accessibility & SEO Basics

Why It Matters

Accessibility (a11y) means everyone can use your page: people using screen readers, keyboards only, zoomed text, or slow connections. SEO (Search Engine Optimization) helps search engines understand your page. The good news: both mostly come from writing clean, semantic HTML.

Write Good Alt Text

ImageBad altGood alt
Photo of a graduationalt="image1"alt="Students throwing caps at graduation"
Search icon buttonalt="icon"alt="Search"
Purely decorative linealt="line"alt="" (empty, so it is skipped)

Describe the purpose of the image, not the file name.

Headings and Landmarks

  • Use one h1 per page.
  • Do not skip levels (h2 then h4).
  • Use header, nav, main, footer so screen reader users can jump around.
  • Set the language: <html lang="en">.
<header>...</header>
<nav>...</nav>
<main>
  <h1>Page title</h1>
  <section>
    <h2>Section title</h2>
  </section>
</main>
<footer>...</footer>

Links, Buttons and Forms

  • Link text should make sense alone: "Read the HTML guide", not "Click here".
  • Use a real button for actions and a for navigation. A div with a click handler cannot be reached with the keyboard.
  • Every input needs a label.
  • Make sure text has enough colour contrast with its background.

ARIA in One Minute

ARIA attributes add meaning when native HTML is not enough. The first rule of ARIA: use a native element if one exists.

<button aria-label="Close menu">X</button>
<div role="alert">Your changes were saved.</div>
<span aria-hidden="true">decorative star</span>
  • aria-label gives an element a name.
  • role describes what an element is.
  • aria-hidden="true" hides decoration from screen readers.

SEO Basics in the <head>

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Learn HTML | Learning Hub</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Free HTML lessons for beginners with examples and quizzes.">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Learn HTML | Learning Hub">
</head>
  • title is the blue link in search results (keep it under about 60 characters).
  • meta description is the short text under it.
  • viewport makes the page work properly on phones.
  • Open Graph tags (og:) control how your link looks when shared.
